title: Course finale
sub: Questions from the whole course, an answer out loud, two coding tasks and practice in Unity
cards/0/q: Interviewer: “Are Burst and the Job System the same thing?” Which answer is accurate?
cards/0/options/0: No. The Job System hands work to worker threads and tracks dependencies; Burst compiles HPC# via LLVM into optimized machine code. They are independent: Burst also compiles static methods marked [BurstCompile], and a job runs without Burst too
cards/0/options/1: Yes: Burst is the scheduler that runs jobs
cards/0/options/2: Burst is required for jobs to run on worker threads at all
cards/0/options/3: The Job System compiles the code, and Burst spreads it over the cores
cards/0/explain: Two different things: threads and a scheduler versus a compiler. They work best together — a job under Burst — but each is useful alone.
cards/0/wrong/1: The Job System schedules. Burst is a compiler; it has nothing to do with threads.
cards/0/wrong/2: A job without [BurstCompile] still runs on worker threads, just as plain C#.
cards/0/wrong/3: The other way round: threads are the Job System, compilation is Burst.
cards/1/q: Which line stops this job from compiling under Burst?
cards/1/explain: string is a managed type, and Burst does not accept such fields. If the job really needs a name, store a FixedString such as FixedString64Bytes; better still, keep strings out of number crunching.
cards/2/q: Two jobs are scheduled with no dependency, and both write to the same NativeArray. What is true? Select all that apply.
cards/2/options/0: In the Editor the safety system throws an exception when the second job is scheduled
cards/2/options/1: In a build the safety checks are unavailable: the race silently corrupts data
cards/2/options/2: The fix is to pass the first job’s JobHandle to the second one’s Schedule, or to split the data
cards/2/options/3: [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction] on the field removes the race
cards/2/explain: The safety system catches the race only in the Editor; a build has no such checks, and the bug shows up as corrupted data. The disabling attribute removes the check, not the race. ScheduleBatchedJobs only wakes the threads and sets no order.
cards/3/task: Movers computes velocities and integrates positions, but waits for each job right after Schedule. Restructure it: IntegrateJob is scheduled with VelocityJob’s JobHandle as its dependency, the final JobHandle is kept in a field, JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after scheduling, and Complete() goes into LateUpdate. In IntegrateJob mark velocities with [ReadOnly].
cards/3/checks/1/label: IntegrateJob is scheduled with VelocityJob’s JobHandle
cards/3/checks/2/label: The JobHandle is kept in a class field
cards/3/explain: The dependency guarantees order without a main-thread wait: IntegrateJob starts as soon as VelocityJob finishes. Complete() on the last link in LateUpdate completes the whole chain. [ReadOnly] on velocities lets other jobs read that array in parallel. Out loud: “a chain through dependsOn, no Complete() between the links; schedule early, complete late”.
cards/4/q: A buffer of 10,000 elements is needed every frame for the whole match. Which allocator, and how do you handle it?
cards/4/options/0: Persistent: allocate once (in Awake or OnEnable), reuse every frame, free with Dispose() in OnDestroy
cards/4/options/1: TempJob: a new one every frame; it lives up to 4 frames, which is enough
cards/4/options/2: Temp: allocate on the main thread and pass it to the job
cards/4/options/3: Persistent, and no Dispose is needed — Unity frees the memory on exit
cards/4/explain: A long-lived buffer is best allocated once: Persistent is slower to allocate, but you allocate it only once. A Persistent buffer that is never freed is a leak, and leak detection will warn about it.
cards/4/wrong/1: It works, but it allocates and frees 10,000 elements every frame for data that lives the whole match.
cards/4/wrong/2: A main-thread Temp allocation cannot be passed into a job.
cards/4/wrong/3: That is a leak: leak detection reports it, and the memory stays taken.
cards/5/q: A parallel job stores id → cell pairs in a NativeHashMap through AsParallelWriter(), and the code does not compile. Why?
cards/5/options/0: In Collections 2.x NativeHashMap has no ParallelWriter: parallel writes need NativeParallelHashMap
cards/5/options/3: AsParallelWriter() must be called inside Execute
cards/5/explain: In Collections 2.x the old NativeHashMap was renamed to NativeParallelHashMap, and the new NativeHashMap is single-threaded. Set the capacity for a ParallelWriter up front: the container cannot grow during parallel writes.
cards/5/wrong/1: That attribute allows writing to other indices of a NativeArray; it does not add a method to a container.
cards/5/wrong/2: NativeArray is exactly the one without a ParallelWriter; NativeList, NativeQueue and NativeParallelHashMap have one.
cards/5/wrong/3: You get the writer outside and pass it into the job as a field.
cards/6/q: An IJobParallelFor over 100,000 elements, Execute adds two float3 values. Which batchSize do you start with?
cards/6/options/0: 32–128: the work is light, and tiny batches get eaten by work-stealing overhead; then tune it in the Profiler
cards/6/options/1: 1: that keeps the threads evenly loaded
cards/6/explain: Unity recommends 32–128 for simple work, and a small batchSize, down to 1, only for very heavy work. The exact value comes from measuring.
cards/6/wrong/1: For heavy iterations, yes; for adding two vectors, stealing one iteration at a time costs more than the work itself.
cards/6/wrong/2: One batch is taken by one thread: no parallelism.
cards/6/wrong/3: batchSize is the number of iterations in one portion; it is not tied to the core count.
cards/7/task: DamageJob works over an array of Unit structs and branches on an if. Rewrite it as SoA and branch-free: three NativeArray<float> fields named damage, armor and health (damage and armor [ReadOnly]), damage halved when armor > 0, chosen with math.select. The job stays an IJobFor with [BurstCompile]; there must be no Unit struct in the job.
cards/7/checks/1/label: There are NativeArray<float> damage, armor and health
cards/7/checks/3/label: The damage is chosen with math.select
cards/7/checks/4/label: No if and no ternary operator
cards/7/explain: SoA: the loop reads three dense float arrays and does not drag position and rotation through the cache. math.select computes both sides and picks with a mask — a branch-free loop body that Burst can process 4–8 units per instruction. Check it in the Burst Inspector: packed instructions instead of scalar ones in the hot loop.
cards/8/q: Lockstep multiplayer: the simulation must produce bit-identical results on PCs and ARM phones. What do you say about Burst?
cards/8/options/0: FloatMode.Deterministic: supported since Burst 1.8.25 and only on 64-bit platforms, and the inputs and the whole computation path must be deterministic too; otherwise, fixed-point
cards/8/options/1: FloatMode.Fast: it is the same on every platform
cards/8/options/3: Replacing Mathf with Unity.Mathematics is enough
cards/8/explain: Deterministic gives the same result across supported platforms, but only for Burst code and with caveats: non-deterministic input or calls from non-deterministic code break it. Fast, on the contrary, allows reordering and FMA. Precision is about the accuracy of functions, not about matching bits.
cards/8/wrong/1: Fast allows reordering and fused instructions — exactly what makes results differ.
cards/8/wrong/2: FloatPrecision sets the allowed error of functions in ulp, not identical results across CPUs.
cards/8/wrong/3: A math library does not change how the compiler treats floats.
cards/9/q: For every killed unit a system calls EntityManager.DestroyEntity between scheduling two IJobEntity jobs. In the Profiler the main thread waits in the middle of the frame. What do you say?
cards/9/options/0: DestroyEntity is a structural change: main thread, and a sync point that waits for every scheduled job. Record the destruction into an ECB from EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem through a ParallelWriter, right in the job
cards/9/options/1: Put Complete() after each job, so the wait becomes predictable
cards/9/options/2: Make Health enableable — then destruction is free
cards/9/options/3: Move the call into LateUpdate of a separate MonoBehaviour
cards/9/explain: A sync point breaks the parallelism between systems. An ECB moves structural changes to one spot at the end of the group, where jobs are finished anyway, and commands can be recorded from a parallel job.
cards/9/wrong/1: That turns one wait into several.
cards/9/wrong/2: Enableable flips a bit but does not destroy an entity; destruction is still a structural change.
cards/9/wrong/3: It is the same EntityManager on the main thread, just elsewhere; an ECB does it without you picking the moment by hand.
cards/10/q: Explain out loud: “Why is Complete() right after Schedule() bad?” Put the parts of the answer in order.
cards/10/items/0: Mechanism: Schedule() only queues the job and returns a JobHandle — the work runs while the main thread does its own
cards/10/items/1: Problem: with Complete() on the next line the main thread just waits; there is no parallelism with it, and the scheduling is paid for
cards/10/items/2: Rule: schedule early, complete late — Schedule and ScheduleBatchedJobs in Update, Complete in LateUpdate
cards/10/items/3: Check: no long WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread in the Profiler Timeline
cards/10/items/4: Exception: if the result is needed right away and the data is small, Run() is more honest
cards/10/explain: Mechanism → how it breaks → the rule → how you would verify it → when the rule does not apply. That order shows understanding rather than a memorised phrase, and gives the interviewer a place for the next question.
cards/11/title: Practice in Unity: from Update to Burst and back into your answer
cards/11/body:
A 45–60 minute task in a real project: Unity 6 with the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages. The goal is numbers of your own for the answer from the previous lesson.

1. Baseline. A MonoBehaviour holds 100,000 agents in arrays of positions, velocities and targets. Update runs a plain loop: velocity towards the target, a speed clamp with an if, position integration. Wrap the loop in a ProfilerMarker and write down the ms per frame.

2. A job. Move the loop into an IJobFor over Persistent NativeArray<float3>s (allocate in Awake, Dispose in OnDestroy), first without Burst: Schedule(count, default).Complete(). Measure.

3. Burst. Add [BurstCompile]; for Editor measurements turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation. Measure.

4. Parallelism and the frame. ScheduleParallel with batchSize 64, ScheduleBatchedJobs in Update, Complete in LateUpdate. In the Timeline look at the worker threads and at WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread. Try batchSize 1 and 1024.

5. Burst Inspector. Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector, “Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed”. Find the hot loop, replace the if with math.select and compare the instructions.

6. Optional — Entities. The same agents as entities from a baked prefab, with an IJobEntity and ScheduleParallel.

It worked if: the Burst version is several times faster than the managed loop; the wait in LateUpdate is close to zero; the Inspector shows packed instructions in the hot loop; leaving Play Mode gives no leak warnings. Repeat the main measurement in a development build on a device and put “before → after” into the template from the lesson “How to talk about your experience” — now it is your story.
